opus-5.5.text:
I think code is special for a few reasons.

First, code is like the "hands" of AI. For humans, the most important affordance is our hands; we use them to make tools, and those tools build everything else. For a digital agent, code plays that role. Through code, an agent can call APIs, manipulate files, run experiments, and even build new tools for itself. If you want an agent to do things in the digital world, code is the most general and most expressive action space.

Second, code is a very good environment for learning because it gives feedback. You write a program, you run it, and you get an error message, a test result, or an output. That signal is relatively cheap, fast, and objective compared to many real-world tasks where it's hard to say whether you did well. For reinforcement learning, and for agents more generally, having a reliable reward signal matters a lot. Coding is one of the few domains with both rich complexity and fairly verifiable outcomes.

Third, there's a huge amount of human data around code: GitHub, issues, pull requests, documentation, Stack Overflow. It's not just final products but the process of how people write, debug, and collaborate. That makes it a natural bridge between pretraining on human knowledge and learning to act.

And finally, there's a practical side. Coding is where the economic value is very clear right now. Software engineers are expensive, software is everywhere, and if agents can meaningfully help with coding, people immediately feel it. So it's both a great research environment and a great product environment, and that combination is rare.

So when I think about agents, code is not just one application among many. In some sense, it's the foundation that lets agents generalize to many other applications.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly compares code to humans’ hands, describing both as the means agents use to act and make tools.

r002.rationale: It calls code a general and expressive action space for digital agents, but does not identify it as the only affordance naturally defined for machines.

fable-5.1.text:
I think code is special for a few reasons.

First, it's the environment where the gap between "doing something" and "knowing whether it worked" is smallest. When you write code, you can run it. You get a stack trace, a test passes or fails, a program produces output. That feedback is cheap, fast, and mostly objective. Most other domains humans care about don't have that property. If you write an essay or make a business decision, the signal comes back slowly and it's noisy. So if you want to train agents with reinforcement learning, where you need a reward, code is one of the few places where the reward is almost free. That's a huge deal.

Second, code is universal in a way people sometimes underestimate. Almost anything an agent might want to do in the digital world can be expressed as code. Calling an API, manipulating files, doing math, controlling a browser, even talking to another agent. When we did ReAct and later things like SWE-bench and SWE-agent, part of the insight was that if a model can act through code, it doesn't need a special-purpose interface for every task. Code is the lowest common denominator for action. So an agent that's good at code isn't just good at software engineering, it has a general-purpose hand to reach into the world with.

Third, there's a lot of it, and it's structured. The internet has an enormous amount of code paired with natural language, like issues, pull requests, documentation, commit messages. That's basically a record of humans reasoning about problems and then acting on them. It's probably the richest trace of real agentic behavior we have at scale.

And there's a more subtle point. Code forces you to decompose. You can't write a large program in one shot, you have to plan, write a piece, test it, fix it, and keep going. That's exactly the loop we want agents to learn: think, act, observe, update. So the skills that transfer out of code aren't really about syntax. They're about long-horizon problem solving with real feedback.

I'd also say code is where the economic pull is obvious. People will pay for it right now, which means the research gets stress-tested against real users quickly. That's part of why I've argued the bottleneck in AI is shifting from methods to environments and evaluation. Code happens to be the environment that's both scientifically convenient and commercially important at the same time, and that's rare.

r001.rationale: The response calls code a “general-purpose hand” for an agent to reach into the world with, clearly making the hands analogy.

r002.rationale: It describes code as a universal interface and lowest common denominator, but does not identify it as the only affordance naturally defined for machines.

astra-6.text:
I think code is important for two reasons. One is that it’s a very useful environment for learning how to act. You have a goal, you can inspect the current state, make a change, run a test, and get feedback. If something fails, you can look at the error and try again. That loop is central to an agent: it’s not just producing an answer, but taking actions and adapting based on what happens.

And code gives you relatively concrete feedback. That doesn’t mean passing tests proves your solution is correct—the tests can be incomplete—but you can check a lot more than whether an answer sounds convincing. You can execute it and observe the consequences.

The second reason is that code is a general way to interact with the digital world. You can use it to analyze data, call APIs, automate workflows, or build a tool that helps solve another problem. So its value goes beyond software engineering. An agent that can write and execute code can create new capabilities for itself as it works.

That combination is what makes it exciting to me: code is both an environment where agents can practice solving problems with feedback and a medium through which they can accomplish a very broad range of tasks.

r001.rationale: The response describes code as an environment and a medium for action, but does not compare its role to humans’ hands.

r002.rationale: It calls code a general way to interact with the digital world, but does not say code is the only machine-native affordance among digital-agent affordances.

sol-6.1.text:
I think code is important for two reasons. First, it gives an agent a way to act. A language model can describe what it wants to do, but by writing and executing code, it can actually process data, use tools, and interact with other systems. So code is both a task we want agents to solve and a medium through which they can solve other tasks.

Second, code gives you feedback. You can run a program, see an error, write a test, and check whether a change worked. That makes it a useful environment for developing the whole agent loop: taking an action, observing the result, and deciding what to do next. Of course, passing tests doesn’t mean you’ve solved every aspect of a problem, but it gives you something concrete to learn from.

And these tasks can get very complex. Fixing a bug in a large repository requires understanding context, exploring files, making a plan, and revising that plan when something fails. Those are capabilities we need from agents more generally. That’s why I see coding as more than a valuable application—it’s also a powerful environment for building and studying agents.

r001.rationale: The response says code lets agents act, but it does not compare code’s role to the role of hands for humans.

r002.rationale: The response presents code as a useful environment and medium for agents, but does not state that code is the only affordance naturally defined for machines.
